name: Weave Intro Tutorial 1.1
description: Practical Weave Deck intro 1.1: dynamic card types, sourcing, AI/parse preview, study UI, and common workflows.

cards.content:
What is Weave Deck’s learning loop?

---div---

Excerpt → create cards → review → quiz → source back.

Take key points from notes or reading into memory cards, reinforce them with spaced repetition, quiz when needed; during review you can still jump back to the original context instead of keeping only isolated sentences.

#weave-tutorial #learning-loop

Why keep memory cards in separate decks instead of writing everything into the source note?

---div---

Source notes stay for reading and writing; cards are managed and scheduled for review on their own. Both sides stay linked by sourcing—jump back when you need context.

That keeps notes clean while collecting “things to remember” in one place.

#weave-tutorial #cards-and-notes

What is the biggest difference between Weave’s card-type system and many Anki-style plugins?

---div---

Weave has no fixed “pick a template first, then fill fields” model. You write Markdown in the card; the plugin dynamically parses special markers and previews different types. Change the markers, and detection/preview follow.

Many Anki-style plugins pick Q&A / multiple-choice templates first, then fill fixed fields. In Weave the card body is the source of truth—that is dynamic card types.

#weave-tutorial #dynamic-card-types

In roughly what order does the plugin detect card types?

---div---

1. Cloze markers (e.g. ==text== or {{c1::text}}) → cloze / fill-in  
2. Else, at least two lettered options (A. B. C. …) → multiple choice  
3. Else → Q&A (often split front/back with ---div---)

Write the markers for the type you want—you do not “choose a template” first.

#weave-tutorial #type-detection

How do you usually split the front and back of a Q&A card?

---div---

Use ---div---:

- Above: question (shown first in review)  
- Below: answer and extras  

Without a separator, the whole text often stays on the front and the back feels empty—“flip to nothing”.

#weave-tutorial #qa-cards

Official Weave Q&A sample—paste into a new card to preview.

What is the core idea of spaced repetition?

---div---

Review just as you are about to forget, following the forgetting curve.

Hint: spaced repetition builds on the Ebbinghaus curve—reviewing near the point of decay strengthens long-term memory.

> Note: ---div--- puts the question above and the answer below; “Hint” is extra text, not another card-type syntax.

#weave-tutorial #official-sample #qa-cards

What must a multiple-choice card make clear?

---div---

Stem, options, and the correct answer; explanation optional.

- Options: A. B. C. D. with a letter and a period (at least two lines)  
- Answer: parentheses at the end of the stem, e.g. (B) or (AC); or Answer: B  
- Explanation: after ---div---  

Missing option lines usually fails MC detection; unmarked answers make scoring unreliable.

#weave-tutorial #multiple-choice

Official Weave multiple-choice sample—paste into a new card to preview.

In FSRS, what does “S” stand for? (B)

A. Speed
B. Stability
C. Strength
D. Success

---div---

S means Stability—one of FSRS’s core parameters.

> Format note: (B) at the end of the stem is the correct answer; A.–D. are standard options; text under ---div--- is explanation for after flip, not part of option scoring. Swap stem/options the same way for other items.

#weave-tutorial #official-sample #multiple-choice

Which two cloze / fill-in markers are commonly used?

---div---

1. Obsidian highlight: ==hidden content==  
2. Anki-style: {{c1::hidden content}}; with a hint: {{c1::answer::hint}}  

Once these markers appear, the type tends to resolve as cloze. If you meant Q&A, do not leave cloze markers behind.

#weave-tutorial #cloze

Official Weave cloze sample—paste into a new card to preview.

FSRS predicts the ==optimal review interval== by computing two core parameters of a card: ==stability== (Stability) and ==difficulty== (Difficulty).

Hint: stability reflects how well memory holds; difficulty reflects how hard the material is to remember. Together they drive the next interval.

> Note: text inside == == is hidden during study; English in parentheses is visible commentary. Keep or edit the hint as you like.

#weave-tutorial #official-sample #cloze

If preview shows a different type than you intended, what should you check first?

---div---

1. Meant Q&A but left A. B. option lines → becomes multiple choice  
2. Meant Q&A but left == == or {{c1::}} → becomes cloze  
3. Meant multiple choice but only used - lists or checkboxes, no A. B. → often fails MC detection  

Clear leftover markers and preview usually follows immediately.

#weave-tutorial #type-troubleshooting

Which statement about “dynamic card types” is correct? (B)

A. You must pick a template in settings or the type will keep changing  
B. Change the markers in the body and detection/preview follow  
C. Only cards imported from APKG support dynamic types  
D. Once saved, the type is locked forever

---div---

Weave treats body markers as the source of truth: change the writing, change the detection.

#weave-tutorial #dynamic-card-types

What is image occlusion, and when does it help?

---div---

Cover regions on an image in a card; during study, recall first, then reveal (via “Show answer” for all, or tap one mask).

Good for anatomy plates, diagrams, and map labels—“where is it?” tasks. For text keywords, prefer ==cloze== or {{c1::}}.

Starter path: put an image in the card → place the cursor on the image line → editor menu / command “Weave Deck image occlusion”. Details: official website tutorials.

#weave-tutorial #image-occlusion

What is a vocabulary card, and how do people usually add one?

---div---

A card shaped around “headword + pronunciation/definition + audio”, often with auto-play during review.

Common path: install community plugin fingertip translation → look up a selection → “Add to Weave Deck” in the popup and pick a deck.

US/UK defaults usually follow fingertip settings; in study “More”, enable “Auto-play media”.

#weave-tutorial #vocabulary-cards

What are the everyday ways to create a card?

---div---

1. Desktop floating “New card” button (toggle in settings)  
2. Command palette: new / selection-based create commands  
3. New-card entries on card management, decks, and similar UI  
4. Main UI “AI card creation”: chat/generate or parse preview, then import  
5. External import: CSV / legacy APKG (menu labels as shown in the plugin)  

Start with the floating button; for long material or already-formatted notes, try AI card creation / parse preview.

#weave-tutorial #create-entry-points

How do you create a card with the desktop floating button?

---div---

1. Click floating “New card”  
2. Write content in the modal (paste an official sample to experiment)  
3. Confirm the deck and save  

Missing the button? Plugin settings → Basic → turn on “Show floating create button”.

#weave-tutorial #floating-create

What does “Pin” at the top of the new-card modal do?

---div---

With pin on, saving a card **does not close** the modal, so you can write the next one immediately.

Useful for a burst of cards on one topic, or continuous excerpts with PDF++. Unpin when you do not need a streak.

#weave-tutorial #pin #floating-create

When is the command palette or an in-UI button better than the floating button?

---div---

- You already selected text in a note and want a block-ref card → selection commands are more direct  
- You are already in card management and want a quick new card → use the page toolbar  
- Mobile, or you dislike the floating ball → command palette is steadier  

Different doors, same goal: open an editor and turn a point into a card.

#weave-tutorial #create-entry-points

In the new-card modal, how do you confirm you wrote the type you want?

---div---

Watch preview while writing: cloze markers → cloze; A. B. options → multiple choice; ---div--- front/back without those markers → Q&A.

Write the content clearly first, then confirm the type in preview—better than fretting over “which template”.

#weave-tutorial #card-preview #dynamic-card-types

What problem does “AI card creation” solve, and how does it differ from hand-written new cards?

---div---

Hand a note (or a passage) to a model to draft many cards; inspect and pick in a preview area, then import into a deck.

Best when material is long and needs summarization. Hand-written new cards fit when the point is already clear and you want one precise card at a time.

Open via main UI top-left menu → **AI card creation** (or the AI assistant entry—follow on-screen labels). Configure AI services in settings first; generation stays unavailable until configured—details in settings and website tutorials.

#weave-tutorial #ai-cards

How does “Parse preview” differ from “AI card creation”?

---div---

- **Parse preview**: split **already-written** card bodies from a note with separators / regex templates, preview, then import—**no** model call required.  
- **AI card creation / AI chat**: the model **generates** drafts from material; usually needs your own API (Premium—follow in-plugin labels).  

Both often live on the same “AI card creation” page via top switches. Notes already in clean Q&A/cloze layout → prefer parse preview; long prose that needs summarization → use AI.

#weave-tutorial #parse-preview #ai-cards

What problem does block-reference card creation mainly solve?

---div---

Keep a deck card aligned with a specific note passage: select text → create a block link → fill the new-card modal. During review you can source-jump to the exact place.

Notes keep writing; cards keep remembering—without shredding the note into flashcard debris.

#weave-tutorial #block-refs

How do you use the command “Create card from selection with block embed”?

---div---

1. Select the text to card in Markdown  
2. Run “Create card from selection with block embed” from the command palette  
3. The plugin writes a block id and opens the new-card modal  
4. Confirm the auto-filled block embed; add answer, cloze, or explanation if needed  
5. Save into a deck  

No selection → you are asked to select first; the source must be Markdown.

#weave-tutorial #block-ref-create

After block-ref create, what does a typical embed look like, and what does it mean?

---div---

Common shape:

![[Note path#^blockId]]

It ties the card to the paragraph that has that block id. You can still write Q&A, cloze, or explanation around it; the embed “anchors” the source.

#weave-tutorial #block-embed

Why source-jump during review? Can you delete ^blockId in the source note?

---div---

Sourcing returns you to original context so you remember meaning, not only the sentence on the card.

^blockId is the anchor—do not delete it casually, or jumps may coarsen or break. If you only open the whole note and miss the paragraph, the block link was probably never created—still usable, just coarser.

#weave-tutorial #sourcing

Besides block embeds, how else can you add a source to a card?

---div---

When creating/editing a card, fill the YAML (properties) field **we_source** with a source link.

Common values (compatibility as implemented):

- Obsidian note / heading / block links  
- PDF++ excerpt links  
- Excalidraw, Weave Reader, and similar material links  
- External URLs  

On save, the plugin parses this into card sourcing. Block embeds fit “body stays in sync with the source passage”; `we_source` fits PDF clips, reader positions, and URLs where a block embed may not apply.

#weave-tutorial #sourcing #we_source

Which best describes body vs source when creating from a block ref? (B)

A. You must copy the whole passage into the card or you cannot review  
B. Block embed / sourcing keeps alignment; the card can still hold Q&A or cloze  
C. Once carded, the source paragraph is locked by the plugin  
D. Only multiple-choice cards support block refs

---div---

The link handles alignment and jump-back; the card can still organize what you need to remember with dynamic types.

#weave-tutorial #block-refs

What is a formal deck, and any tips when creating one?

---div---

A formal deck is a “study basket” you create on purpose—cards for one theme live together.

Name is required; tags are optional. Prefer course / book / exam-subject groupings instead of one endless mega-deck.

#weave-tutorial #formal-decks

Can one card belong to multiple decks? Why help?

---div---

Yes (reference membership).

The same card can sit in “Daily review” and “Pre-exam sprint” without duplicating the body; edit once, every reference sees the same card.

#weave-tutorial #deck-membership

How do formal decks differ from emergent decks?

---div---

- **Formal deck**: you create it and put cards in—clear ownership, good for long-term subjects/books.  
- **Emergent deck**: an auto-assembled study view by **tags and rules**, good for temporarily gathering cards without hand-moving them.

Formal = “I build the basket”; emergent = “rules fire, cards gather”. Emergent may be Premium—follow in-plugin labels.

#weave-tutorial #formal-decks #emergent-decks

Where do memory-deck study data mainly live? What should sync across devices?

---div---

By default inside the vault—commonly `.wdeck` files under weave/memory/, traveling with whatever syncs the vault.

Caches and local state under the plugin directory usually should not be treated as study data to sync. For multi-device study, keep vault decks and related notes consistent first.

#weave-tutorial #data-location #sync

Is it safe to rename or delete .wdeck / .qbank in a file manager?

---div---

Not in bulk, and not casually, unless you know the consequences.

Use in-plugin deck and data management. If files and internal membership drift apart, decks can look empty, cards “vanish”, or progress mismatches. For backups, copying Weave-related vault folders is usually safer than picking files one by one.

#weave-tutorial #data-safety

What does per-deck “Memory Config” roughly do?

---div---

Bind review-related templates/parameters (e.g. target retention) to **one memory deck**, instead of forcing one setting for the whole library.

Open “Memory Config” from the deck menu or related deck settings, choose, and confirm. Defaults are fine at first; tune when a subject is clearly harder/easier. Details follow in-plugin help.

#weave-tutorial #memory-config

What is the main difference between memory decks and question banks? (B)

A. Only question banks can source back to notes  
B. Memory decks focus on spaced review; question banks focus on drills and quiz verification  
C. File formats are identical; only the UI name differs  
D. Basic experience cannot use any quiz-related ability

---div---

`.wdeck` memory decks serve “remember”; `.qbank` question banks serve “test yourself”. Document quizzes can also parse Markdown into a session. Full banks and some analytics may be Premium—follow labels; for onboarding, get memory decks fluent first.

#weave-tutorial #memory-decks #question-banks

Which analytics charts do memory decks support, and what for?

---div---

All of these target **memory decks** (separate from question-bank analytics):

- **Retention** (basic): memory rate and recall trends—“how much still sticks”.  
- **Deck profile**: a bird’s-eye composition/status view.  
- **Card count**: scale and structure over time.  
- **Tag difficulty**: difficulty distribution by tag.  
- **Load forecast**: whether upcoming review load looks too heavy.  
- **Calibration**: ratings vs actual recall—too easy/hard grading.  
- **Review timing**: early / on-time / late distribution.  

Later items are often advanced charts—availability follows Basic / Premium labels in the plugin.

#weave-tutorial #analytics #memory-decks

What do the four rating buttons mean?

---div---

- **Again**: blank / fully wrong—should return soon  
- **Hard**: recalled, but with struggle  
- **Good**: normal recall (most common)  
- **Easy**: too easy—longer interval is fine  

The algorithm schedules the next appearance from your choice.

#weave-tutorial #ratings

Why should you not keep pressing “Good” when you did not remember?

---div---

Intervals stretch; you only notice the miss when the card is truly due. Use **Again** when you failed—short-term ugly, long-term cheaper.

Just report whether you could recall in that moment; FSRS6 owns the spacing.

#weave-tutorial #ratings

How do new cards differ from due cards?

---div---

- **New**: first exposure, build an initial imprint  
- **Due**: returned by schedule, check if you still remember  

Open a deck and follow the UI—you do not need every algorithm term first.

#weave-tutorial #study-queue

What if you rate by mistake?

---div---

Prefer Undo on the UI (when offered) immediately so a wrong interval is not written into the schedule.

Habit: glance at the predicted next interval after rating; if it looks absurd, undo and re-rate.

#weave-tutorial #undo-rating

Which study display modes exist, and when to use each?

---div---

On desktop, switch under study side “More” (mobile usually stays on a tab):

1. **Floating modal** (**desktop default**): centered window, not full screen—good while glancing at notes beside it.  
2. **Tab view**: a normal Obsidian tab, easy to park next to other tabs.  
3. **Fullscreen overlay (immersive)**: covers the workspace for focused due-card runs.

Three shells, one study UI. Your choice is remembered; switch again under “More” anytime.

#weave-tutorial #study-ui #display-modes

What is “Study ahead”, and what are the rules?

---div---

**Use**: before travel or exams, pull cards that are **not due yet but will be soon**, so they do not pile up later.

**Rules (essentials)**:

- Includes **already due** cards plus cards due within a **future day window**.  
- “Max advance days” is in study-related settings; everyday **1–3 days** is sensible, hard cap **5**, to avoid borrowing too much future load.  
- Pick a deck first; if nothing is advanceable, you get a “no cards to study ahead” notice.

Study ahead is a bounded borrow—not “clear the entire future queue”.

#weave-tutorial #study-ahead

Can you hide “Question” / “Answer” style labels in the study UI?

---div---

Yes.

Study side toolbar → **More** → find something like **Show content labels**, then toggle question/answer section labels.

Turn off for a cleaner look; turn on when teaching or inspecting structure.

#weave-tutorial #study-ui #content-labels

What does “Recycle” in the study side toolbar do?

---div---

Recycle tags the current card (e.g. `#回收` / `#recycle`) and **temporarily removes it from the study queue**.

- The card is not deleted; content remains.  
- Good for “badly written—don’t bother me in review; I’ll fix later”.  
- After fixing, remove the recycle tag to re-enter study.

Recycle means “hold for improvement”, not delete.

#weave-tutorial #recycle #study-ui

What can you commonly do inside the memory study UI?

---div---

Side toolbar and related menus usually include (follow the live UI):

- **Edit / preview** the card body  
- **Delete** (more permanent than recycle)  
- **Recycle** (park out of queue to fix later)  
- **Undo** the last rating  
- **Reminders** (higher priority when due)  
- **Priority / star-like** marks (if the UI exposes Priority)  
- **Deck membership** or related ordering options  
- **Auto-play audio/media** (on/off; first vs all; on card change or on show answer)  
- **Source / source-block text**, card details, timers, and similar  

Buttons may sit on the main bar or under “More”; desktop can also switch display mode.

#weave-tutorial #study-ui #card-actions

How do you “draw” in memory study? Does Weave ship its own drawing engine?

---div---

Weave does **not** ship a separate drawing engine; it cooperates with **Excalidraw** and similar community plugins:

1. Draw in Excalidraw  
2. Select what you need; use context actions to **group and create a render link**  
3. Insert that link into the card document  

Weave shows it via Obsidian rendering habits. Install and learn Excalidraw when you need drawings; Weave embeds the link into the study flow.

#weave-tutorial #excalidraw #study-ui

How do you add a “hint” on a card during memory study?

---div---

Hints use **Obsidian footnotes**, not a custom hint syntax.

Write footnote refs and definitions in the card Markdown (e.g. `[^1]` and `[^1]: hint text`). Study/preview shows them the Obsidian way—same as notes, carried by official rendering.

#weave-tutorial #hints #footnotes

Why does Weave still support Anki-style cloze {{c1::}}?

---div---

Two main reasons:

1. **Habit**: many users already know Anki cloze; reusing it is cheaper.  
2. **Progressive cloze**: when progressive cloze is detected, Anki-numbered cloze is the authority and stays **separate** from `==highlight==` cloze so the two syntaxes do not collide in one progressive pipeline.

Everyday cloze can use either; for progressive cloze, write Anki-numbered cloze (progressive may be Premium—follow labels).

#weave-tutorial #cloze #anki-cloze #progressive-cloze

When the deck-study view moves between the main pane and a sidebar, how does the default layout differ?

---div---

- **Main pane** → kanban (multi-column overview)  
- **Sidebar** → grid cards (narrower, easier to read)  

Same feature, position-adapted—not two unrelated pages. With auto-switch on, dragging back to the center returns to kanban. Toggle “auto-switch by position” in Basic settings.

#weave-tutorial #deck-study #layout

Which views are common in card management, and what for?

---div---

Switch at the top of **Card management** (mobile may use colored dots):

1. **Table**: bulk browse, search/filter, sort, inline edit, batch tidy (often the default).  
2. **Grid**: card-like scan of content and badges.  
3. **Kanban**: column drag (e.g. by status).  
4. **Timeline**: date groups inside **grid layout** to review recent deposits (may be Premium—follow labels).  

Deck study asks “which deck?”; card management asks “which card?”.

#weave-tutorial #card-management #views

Why does the card-management top bar look different in the main pane vs an Obsidian sidebar?

---div---

The two placements serve different intents:

- **Main pane**: browse, manage, process cards—so the bar expands for batch/admin actions.  
- **Sidebar**: watch “what cards grew from the active document”, search related cards—so the bar collapses and keeps sidebar-first tools visible.

You can treat sidebar card management as an inspiration inbox: while reading/editing Markdown, create cards sourced to that note; enable “Filter by active document” to see memory cards, bank-related cards, and sparks already tied to it.

Fewer sidebar buttons means narrow-layout folding, not missing features—drag the view back to the main pane for the full toolbar.

#weave-tutorial #card-management #layout #inspiration

What does “Filter by active document” in card management do?

---div---

It filters to cards whose sourcing links point at the current active document.

As you switch files in the main pane—Markdown, Canvas, books in a reader—the sidebar grid follows and shows related cards, so you immediately see what already exists for this document.

#weave-tutorial #filter-active-document #card-management

How can you lay out the sidebar to write a note while watching “what cards this note has spawned”?

---div---

Put card management in a left/right sidebar, enable “Filter by active document”, keep writing or reading in the center.

Switching the active document refreshes the sidebar grid; jump back to the source when needed. Good while deep-reading a chapter or drafting a long note to catch missing cards or sparks.

#weave-tutorial #filter-active-document #workflow

What is “Important Schedule” for?

---div---

A main-UI hub that gathers study, exam, reading, and note-related plans in one place (commonly calendar on top, list below).

Use it to answer “what today?” at a glance instead of diving into each module. Reading plans and exam arrangements can also surface here. Details follow the live UI.

#weave-tutorial #important-schedule

How do you embed a deck-study view into a normal Markdown note?

---div---

In the note editor, right-click → **Weave Deck actions** → **Insert deck view** → check memory decks → insert.

You get a `weave-decks` code block; Reading / Live Preview renders clickable deck cards. Good for course notes, review checklists, and dashboards.

Embeds **memory decks**, not question banks. This is different from dragging the plugin main window into a sidebar.

#weave-tutorial #insert-deck-view

Which editor does the plugin use?

---div---

Obsidian’s official editor.

That preserves native editing feel and lets many community plugins that depend on the official editor extend card-editing scenarios (compatibility varies by plugin).

#weave-tutorial #official-editor

How does card preview render?

---div---

Obsidian’s official rendering engine.

Formulas, highlights, and common Markdown stay closer to notes; many render/theme community plugins often apply to card preview automatically. Writing a card feels like a short note; viewing it uses the same render stack as notes.

#weave-tutorial #official-render

Can you import Anki cards? Any caveats?

---div---

Yes—legacy Anki APKG packages and CSV (plugin import entries; some may be Premium).

Remember Weave is built for **Obsidian workflows**, with emphasis on **source links** and vault notes. Cards unrelated to the current vault and without meaningful sourcing may not be worth bulk import—migrating content ≠ every card deserves a home.

#weave-tutorial #apkg #anki-import #csv

Does Weave support mobile?

---div---

Yes. Weave Deck targets environments where Obsidian runs—**Windows / macOS / Linux / iOS / Android**.

Mobile is tighter: study sessions are usually **tabs**; deck study and card management lean toward compact grids. The core loop (create, review, source) works on mobile; desktop-only floating buttons and some display switches follow the live UI.

#weave-tutorial #mobile #cross-platform
